verdicts.evidence: Sun: Parker, Silverman and Mayor-elect Lewis George, all Transportation Committee members, 'have said they would vote "no" on the bill if it were put to them this week.' Hill Rag: 'as of Tuesday, three of five had indicated opposition.' Two outlets, so FACT fits.
WJLA, Hill Rag, NBC4 and WUSA9 all give 200 per operator and 800 citywide.

Hill Rag: 'The Washington Post reported' the Coalition for Accountability and Road Safety 'spent over $2.6 million on ads opposing the bill'; 'It is not clear who is behind the campaign.' Attribution chain stated as on the page.

CRS R47927: 'After at least 13 intervening days from the first reading, the council must consider and pass the bill a second time.' Dec. 2 through Dec. 14 is 13 intervening days. Council schedule lists legislative meetings Dec. 1 and Dec. 15.

Bloomberg Law (Apr. 24, 2026): Google 'will invest $10 billion in Anthropic PBC, with another $30 billion potentially to follow'; the two are 'partners and rivals'; Google is 'Alphabet Inc.-owned'. Waymo is an Alphabet company (page and all outlets). REPORTED is the weaker tag; two outlets would allow FACT, but a weaker tag is not an overclaim.
Open and real. My attempt to open lims.dccouncil.gov/Legislation/B26-0684 also failed (robots disallowed), and no outlet links a posted committee print.

Sidley: 'a nonrefundable application fee of US$1 million' and 'an additional US$5 million permit fee', 'the total cost of a three-year permit to US$6 million'. Reason: '$6 million for a three-year permit'. Hill Rag: '$1 million in the introduced bill', 'the earlier $5 million operating-permit fee'. FACT fits.

WJLA: 7.5 cents per mile. Hill Rag: 'a 7.5-cent tax per vehicle mile, half the originally proposed rate.' City Cast's conflicting 20 cents is disclosed in the table note.

Sidley: after administrative costs the bill 'directs half of the remaining revenue to support public transit'; the other half to 'education and workforce training programs' for ride-share drivers at risk of displacement.

Hill Rag: 'After implementation costs, half the fund's revenue would support transit'; 'For the first three years, 25 percent would fund training...' and '25 percent would support accessibility'; 'After three years, the workforce allocation would end and accessibility would receive half the revenue.' City Cast consistent (25%, three-year cap).
Sidley: 'initially limited to operating 200 vehicles'; after a 'comprehensive plan', DDOT 'may raise the fleet limit above 200 "through rulemaking."' Reason: 'initial 200-vehicle cap'.
WJLA, Hill Rag, NBC4, WUSA9: 200 per operator, 800 citywide.
Sidley describes no labor or organizing provision; Reason likewise. Stated as absence in coverage, not absence in the bill; correctly hedged.
WJLA: drivers and AV maintenance facility workers 'would have the right to organize and bargain collectively'; Hill Rag and Sun the same.

Chamber of Commerce v. Seattle, No. 17-35640 (9th Cir. May 11, 2018): state-action immunity did not shield the ordinance from the Sherman Act claim (dismissal reversed and remanded); dismissal of NLRA preemption claims (Machinists and Garmon) affirmed. Primary document; FACT fits.
Labeled inference; modest ('could draw the same kind of suit').

Texas House bill analysis, SB 2205 (85R, 2017): 'prohibits a political subdivision or a state agency from imposing a franchise or other regulation related to the operation of an automated motor vehicle or automated driving system.' Effective Sept. 1, 2017. Source is a committee bill analysis, not the enacted text.

Round 2 (commit 92373ce): Now 'Where a higher level moves first, it can take the question away from cities, as Texas did.' Labeled inference, rests on SB 2205's bar on local regulation of AV operation; no longer generalizes.

City figures match: Phoenix 76% lower, Los Angeles 71% lower, San Francisco 35% lower, Austin 4% higher (small sample). Primary plus Hill Rag/autoevolution.

IIHS President David Harkey: 'the present data collection system isn't good enough to allow continuous monitoring of a large-scale expansion.' Hill Rag: 'inadequate data collection makes monitoring a broader rollout difficult.'
